children: By Don Nico Forbes and Ed Frankl
For Volkmar Noeske, chief executive of German defense manufacturer Jowa-KLN Group, 2026 has been a challenging year. Just not in the way many economists feared.
As the war in Iran drove up energy prices and threatened fresh disruption for German industry, Noeske has instead been scrambling to keep up with a rush of orders.
"It's been a very intense year. Orders have been strong, with a lot of procurement activity from the government," he said.

Jowa-KLN's experience reflects broader trends across German industry in recent months. Both factory orders and industrial production rose in the second quarter, shaking off fears of a slowdown as disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz sent energy prices soaring.

It comes after years of stagnation in the eurozone's largest economy, whose export-orientated industrial sector hit the buffers. The challenges of stiff Chinese competition, as well as surging energy costs after the cheap Russian gas faucet was turned off during the country's invasion of Ukraine, means production remains below 2019 levels. President Trump's tariff agenda has since added further uncertainty for manufacturers.
But Germany's economy grew last year for the first time since 2022, and a revival in industry is seen by economists as key to getting a recovery back on track.

Industrial momentum is being driven in part by public investment, with the government last year agreeing on a stimulus package worth more than $1 trillion. This has been a particular boon for the defense sector amid hopes that a military buildout could present fresh impetus for industry, while the U.S.'s threatened pullback from its military support for Europe has underscored the need for greater investment.

Adding fresh impetus, the conflict in Ukraine has inflamed tensions across NATO territory in recent months. Last week, Germany accused Russia of planning to send explosive drones to a German airport, and threatened to retaliate.

"The German population is just slowly starting to realize that it's not a war fought in Ukraine. It's something hybrid which is happening here every day… that will support the government's activities on defense spending even further," Noeske said.

But conflict in the Middle East has also given Germany's manufacturers a boost. Many orders came from buyers seeking to stockpile goods in anticipation of further supply-chain disruptions down the line, according to Henrik Meincke, head of economic and industrial policy at VCI, a trade association representing the chemical and pharmaceutical industry in Germany.

In addition, economists have pointed to an uptick in demand due to even greater disruption to manufacturers in Asia from the war in Iran. Exports drove much of the gains in eurozone GDP in the months after the outbreak of the war.
But as Meincke points out, these benefits are likely only short-term, with broader structural issues continuing to weigh on industry.

"If you look at our capacity utilization, it is still very low," he said. "We see overcapacities in China, especially in the chemical sector, which goes to global markets and puts pressure on Europe."

Competitive concerns are also weighing on carmakers, another key industrial sector for Germany. Auto production fell 9.2% on month in July, dragging overall output into negative territory for the first time in four months. Last week, German auto giant Volkswagen approved jobs cuts of 100,000 as it faces stiff competition from China, alongside U.S. tariffs.

The fall in output for July highlights the fragility of a recovery in German industry, with exports also falling in the month for the first time since January. It is a reminder that stockpiling demand won't last forever, with risks of a genuine drag from higher energy prices rising as the war in Iran persists. Still, new orders continued to pick up in July, while export expectations in August jumped to multiyear highs, according to the Ifo Institute.

Key will be how sectors adapt to increasing competition and a new industrial playbook where manufacturing is geared increasingly toward defense--a transition which government stimulus should support. According to Deutsche Bank, the effects of spending are expected to become increasingly visible in the economy later this year and in early 2027.
Yet capital expenditure among German companies remains on the decline, with economists pointing to a lack of reform in the country's complex regulatory system as one factor holding back investment.

"The German economy is like a car with a broken cylinder," said Joerg Kraemer, an economist at Commerzbank. "As long as the necessary far-reaching economic reforms aren't implemented, key private-sector investment is unlikely to increase significantly."

But while challenging for certain sectors, for companies already geared to Germany's new industrial economy, the benefits could be significant. As Noeske noted, Jowa-KLN Group has been able to roughly triple its business in the last few years.
"For us, this is just the beginning of a very new phase," Noeske said. "It's the next decades which we're actually looking forward to."
